hints: Focus on what links the measured mass to the identity of a noble gas, its molar mass.
Use $pV = nRT$ with $p = 101000 \text{ Pa}$, $V = 400 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3$ and $T = 300 \text{ K}$ to find $n$.
Divide the 0.65 g sample mass by your moles to get $M_r$ in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$, then match it to He (4.0), Ne (20.2), Ar (39.9) or Kr (83.8).
walkthrough:
**Find the moles of gas from the ideal gas equation**

We know pressure, volume and temperature, so we can find $n$. Remember to convert to SI units for the calculation.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$pV = nRT \text{ so } n = \frac{pV}{RT}$$

**Put in the numbers carefully**

Volume $400 \text{ cm}^3 = 400 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3 = 4.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^3$. Pressure $101 \text{ kPa} = 101000 \text{ Pa}$.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$n = \frac{101000 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-4}}{8.31 \times 300} = \frac{40.4}{2493} \approx 0.0162 \text{ mol}$$

**Calculate the molar mass and identify the gas**

Molar mass is mass per mole. The tube gained 0.65 g, so that is the mass of 0.0162 mol.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$M_r = \frac{m}{n} = \frac{0.65}{0.0162} \approx 40.1 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$$
This matches argon, $A_r \approx 39.9$, very closely.

options.A: Correct. $M_r \approx 40 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$ matches argon ($A_r = 39.9$). The calculated moles of about 0.0162 mol and mass of 0.65 g give this value perfectly.
options.B: Incorrect. Helium has $M_r = 4.0$. 0.0162 mol of helium would weigh only about 0.065 g, ten times lighter than observed. Choosing this often means forgetting to convert $\text{cm}^3$ to $\text{m}^3$ or $\text{kPa}$ to $\text{Pa}$.
options.C: Incorrect. Krypton has $M_r = 83.8$. 0.0162 mol of krypton would weigh about 1.36 g, roughly double the observed mass. This is too heavy to fit the data.
options.D: Incorrect. Neon has $M_r = 20.2$. 0.0162 mol of neon would weigh about 0.33 g, about half the observed mass. This trap is common if volume is halved or moles are doubled by a unit error.
